1.description: Intermittent gaps where the upper thread fails to interlock with the bobbin thread, leaving missed stitches or broken thread segments.
1.visual_sign: Thread line has missing loops or gaps with visible holes where needle penetrated without locking.

minor.label: Low Severity (Isolated Skip)
minor.impact: Cosmetic imperfection, slight risk of unraveling over repeated wash cycles.

moderate.label: Moderate Severity (Multiple Skips)
moderate.impact: Structural weakness along the seam. Joint may separate under tension.

severe.label: High Severity (Continuous Breakage)
severe.impact: Seam failure. Garment cannot be sold or delivered to client.

root_causes: Needle is blunt, slightly bent, or inserted backwards (flat side in wrong direction).
Mismatch between fabric type and needle point (e.g. using a universal needle instead of ballpoint on jersey knit).
Upper thread tension too high or thread path snagging on spool notch.
Incorrect threading of tension disks or take-up lever.
Bobbin case timing out of sync with needle descent.
tailor_actions: 1. Stop sewing and unthread the defective section using an ergonomic seam ripper.
2. Replace the needle immediately. For knit/spandex fabrics, insert a 75/11 or 80/12 Ballpoint/Stretch needle. For medium cottons, use a fresh 80/12 Universal needle.
3. Verify needle orientation: Ensure the flat side of the shank faces the back (or toward the direction specified by your machine brand).
4. Re-thread the upper thread with presser foot UP to ensure thread seats completely into the tension disks.
5. Overlap the new stitch line by 0.5 inches over the existing good seam and secure with 2-3 reverse lockstitches.
1.preventive_tips: Change sewing machine needles after every 8-10 hours of active sewing or at the start of every new boutique garment.

2.description: Gathering, bunching, or rippling of fabric directly along the stitch line, causing the seam to ripple instead of laying flat.
2.visual_sign: Wrinkles radiating outwards from the stitch line, wavy uneven edges.

minor.label: Minor Wrinkling
minor.impact: Can often be pressed out with a steam iron and tailor's ham.

moderate.label: Noticeable Gathering
moderate.impact: Visible ripples; iron pressing alone is insufficient. Requires tension adjustment.

severe.label: Severe Seam Puckering
severe.impact: Garment distortion; sleeves or side seams pull unevenly.

root_causes: Upper thread tension is set too high relative to bobbin tension.
Needle size is too thick for delicate or lightweight fabric (e.g., chiffon, georgette, silk).
Differential feeding: The machine feed dogs pull the bottom ply faster than the presser foot feeds the top ply.
Stitch length is set too short, causing too many needle penetrations per inch.
Sewing across bias without proper seam stabilization.
tailor_actions: 1. Loosen the upper thread tension dial by 1.0 to 1.5 units (e.g., dial down from 4 to 2.5 or 3).
2. Increase stitch length slightly (e.g., from 2.0mm to 2.5mm or 3.0mm) to reduce fabric displacement.
3. Switch to a finer needle size (65/9 or 70/10 Microtex/Sharp needle for delicate silks and synthetics).
4. Place a strip of lightweight tear-away stabilizer or tissue paper beneath the seam while sewing to prevent feed dog bunching.
5. If present on existing garment, steam press with a damp pressing cloth. If ripples remain, unpick and re-stitch with corrected tension.
2.preventive_tips: Always run a 6-inch test seam on identical scrap fabric of the same grainline before sewing the main garment panels.

3.description: A separation or gaping hole between two stitched fabric panels where the seam has pulled apart or thread has unraveled.
3.visual_sign: Visible opening exposing raw edge allowances or interior garment lining.

minor.label: Minor Gap (< 1 inch)
minor.impact: Early stage failure; can be easily reinforced without restitching entire seam.

moderate.label: Moderate Gap (1 - 3 inches)
moderate.impact: Significant structural opening; skin or underlayer exposed.

severe.label: Major Seam Separation (> 3 inches)
severe.impact: Critical joint failure requiring full disassembly and reinforcement.

root_causes: Lack of proper backtacking (reverse stitching) at seam beginnings and terminations.
Weak, deteriorated, or incorrect weight thread (e.g. basting thread left in structural seam).
Insufficient seam allowance (cut too close to stitch line, causing weave fraying).
Excessive stress or tight fitting on garment seams.
tailor_actions: 1. Turn garment inside out and inspect the remaining seam allowance for fraying.
2. Trim loose, frayed threads neatly without cutting into the seam line.
3. Pin the open seam carefully, matching notches and grainline exactly.
4. Re-sew the seam starting 1 inch before the break, stitch through the open area, and continue 1 inch past the opening.
5. Perform a secure reverse backstitch (3-4 stitches) at both beginning and end.
6. If seam allowance is fraying, finish raw edges with an overlock (serger) stitch or zigzag stitch.
3.preventive_tips: Reinforce high-stress points (crotch seams, armholes, pocket corners) with a double stitch line or bartack.

4.description: Crooked, meandering, or off-parallel stitching that departs from the intended seam allowance line.
4.visual_sign: Wavy stitch line, uneven margin from the fabric edge, mismatch at seam intersections.

minor.label: Slight Drift (< 2mm)
minor.impact: Minor aesthetic variance, usually concealed in inner linings.

moderate.label: Moderate Wavering (2 - 5mm)
moderate.impact: Visible asymmetry on collars, cuffs, hems, or exterior topstitching.

severe.label: Severe Misalignment (> 5mm)
severe.impact: Alters garment fit and creates crooked drape on finished pieces.

root_causes: Operator pulling or pushing fabric by hand instead of letting feed dogs transport it evenly.
Absence of seam guides or failure to watch the needle plate guideline.
Sewing at an excessively high speed without consistent fabric control.
Uneven pinning or fabric shifting between top and bottom plies.
tailor_actions: 1. For exterior or visible topstitching, unpick the wavy segment with a fine seam ripper.
2. Use a tailor's chalk pencil and ruler to draw a crisp guide line on the fabric.
3. Attach a magnetic seam guide or place a strip of low-tack colored masking tape at the desired seam allowance (e.g. 1/2" or 5/8").
4. Reduce sewing machine speed by setting speed limiter to medium-low.
5. Keep eyes focused on the edge of the fabric against the seam guide rather than staring directly at the bouncing needle.
4.preventive_tips: Use walking foot (even feed foot) when stitching multiple layers or slippery fabrics like satin and rayon.

5.description: Punctures, cuts, or chewed yarns along the seam where the needle point severed fabric yarns rather than sliding between them.
5.visual_sign: Small pierced holes, ladders/runs in knit fabrics, frayed yarn cuts along stitch line.

minor.label: Isolated Needle Holes
minor.impact: Small pinholes; fabric may recover with steam pressing or light fusible webbing.

moderate.label: Multiple Yarn Cuts
moderate.impact: Runs/ladders forming in knit loops, risk of tear expansion.

severe.label: Severe Chewed Seam
severe.impact: Fabric disintegrating along seamline; requires structural patch or re-cutting.

root_causes: Using a burred, nicked, or dull needle tip that pierces and cuts warp/weft fibers.
Using a cutting-point needle (designed for leather) on woven or knit fabrics.
Sewing over pins and striking metal, causing microscopic needle hook damage.
Needle plate hole has burrs from previous needle strikes.
tailor_actions: 1. Discard the defective needle immediately to prevent further damage.
2. Check needle plate and bobbin hook for rough burrs; buff smooth with fine crocus cloth if needed.
3. For knits, switch to a Ballpoint (SES) or Stretch needle that parts knit loops gently.
4. For delicate wovens, apply a small strip of lightweight fusible knit interfacing (iron-on) to the reverse side to stabilize yarn cuts.
5. Re-stitch slightly outside the damaged line (increase seam allowance by 1/8") to anchor stitches into undamaged fabric weave.
5.preventive_tips: Never sew directly over pins. Remove each pin just before it reaches the presser foot.
